title: The unaccepted gift
hookLine: abused by a visitor, the Buddha asks: if a gift isn't accepted, whose is it? (Samyutta Nikaya 7.2)

cards: If you bring someone a gift and they don't take it, who owns it? It sounds like a riddle for children. In the Samyutta Nikaya, it's the heart of the Buddha's reply to a man who has just cursed him.
The man is a brahmin of the Bharadvaja clan. He's heard that someone from his clan has left home to become a monk under the Buddha, and he is furious.
So he finds the Buddha and abuses him to his face, with rude and harsh words.

teach.h: WHO OWNS A GIFT NOBODY TAKES?
teach.b: The Buddha doesn't answer the insults, and he doesn't go silent either. He asks: do friends and relatives ever come to visit you? Sometimes, the brahmin says.
Do you offer them something to eat? Sometimes, yes. And if they don't accept it, whose is it then?
If they don't accept it, the brahmin says, it stays mine. The Buddha says, in paraphrase: in the same way, you've abused us, who don't abuse, scolded us, who don't scold, and we don't accept it.
It's yours, brahmin. It's all yours. Then he adds a picture: someone who answers abuse with abuse is like a host and guest sitting down to share a meal.
He won't share that meal. This isn't ignoring the man. The Buddha heard every word, and he answered.
He just refused the role of the one who eats what's served. That leaves the insult exactly where it started.
It also leaves the door open, and the sutta shows it: by the end the brahmin asks to go forth himself, and becomes a monk.
Beside Angulimala, it makes a pair. Yesterday, a man stopped harming. Today, a man stops being harmed, at least in the one way that's up to him: by not swallowing the insult and not throwing it back.
Forgiveness, here, starts as a polite refusal.

how: Buddhist teachers retell this sutta, known as the Akkosa Sutta, when teaching patience: insults are heard but not accepted, and not returned.

o: the village where the Buddha gave his first sermon
the clan of the brahmin whose insults the Buddha declined
the forest where the Buddha met a killer on the road

games.q: the unaccepted gift — tap the pairs.
p: abused the Buddha to his face

s: the Buddha answers the insults with silence
he answers with a question about food offered to guests.
the brahmin later becomes a monk himself
by the end of the sutta he asks to go forth, and is ordained.

games.q: the Buddha asks: you offer food to visiting guests, and they don't accept it. whose is it then?
games.why: it stays with the host. so, the Buddha says, the abuse stays with the man who brought it: it's yours, brahmin.

practice: Bring to mind one insult that has stuck, about your work, your looks, your choices, and picture it as a plate of food set in front of you.

You don't have to eat it, or throw it back across the table; leave it on the plate, let it be carried back to where it came from, and notice your hands, empty. If you pray, you can use your own tradition's words for letting it go.

wordCard.voice: Bharadvaja. The brahmin clan of the man who cursed the Buddha, and whose abuse the Buddha declined to accept. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari: akkosa, abuse or reviling; the sutta is known as the Akkosa Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: yours to keep. The insult stays with the one who brought it. Day nine hundred sixty-four, done.
